title: Numbers and Stories
goal: I can tell what each digit is worth, round numbers, and find the character and setting in a story.

card.desc: Welcome to your own course! First you learn how your course page works. Then you find what each digit is worth, write numbers in expanded form, and round to the nearest ten and hundred. In reading, you find the character and setting in Theo's First Hike and use clues to infer.

win: You found every digit's value and every story clue. Great first lesson, Ce'Line!

slides.title: Welcome to Your Building Blocks!
slides.text:
This course is just for you, Ce'Line. 🧱
We meet one time each week.
Today we learn about numbers and stories.

notes.do: Before class: laptop with this class lesson open (code 9110), her printed Packet (2 pages), a paper place-value mat (three columns: Hundreds, Tens, Ones), base-ten pieces or paper cut-outs (9 hundred squares, 9 ten strips, 9 ones), a small whiteboard and marker, and a pencil. Sit side by side so she can see the screen.
notes.say: Welcome, Ce'Line! This is your very own course. It is called Building Blocks because we build one block at a time. Every Tuesday we learn one new week together.
notes.ask: What is one thing you want to get better at this year?
notes.listen: Any honest answer. Write it on the whiteboard corner and come back to it at the end. Praise her for answering; today is about confidence.

slides.title: How your course works
slides.text: Your course page has one card for each lesson. Here is what is on a card.

steps.text: 📘 Class lesson. We do it together, right now.
💻 After-class lesson. You do it at home on the day of class. It ends with Show What You Know.
🎯 Get 85 or more on Show What You Know. Then your next lesson opens. You can try again. You get new questions each time.
📝 Practice. More questions during the week. You get a new set each time.
🖨️ Packet. Two pages to print. You use a pencil. Do one page at a time.
✅ Task list. One small job each day. Check the box when you finish it.

slides.tip: Three tries on each question. Only your first try counts. So slow down and check.

notes.do: Open her course page in a new tab and show her the Lesson 1 card while you click through the steps. Point to each button: Class Lesson, After-Class Lesson, Practice, Packet. Then point to the task list and the Also do links.
notes.say: You never have to guess what to do. The task list tells you one small job for each day.
notes.ask: Where do you look to see what to do on Thursday?
notes.listen: The task list on her course card. If she says "I don't know", point to it again and have her read the Thursday line out loud.

slides.title: Do you know your course?
slides.text: Answer each one.

items.q: What score on Show What You Know opens your next lesson? Type the number.
items.why: 85 or more opens the next lesson.
items.no: Look back at the step with the 🎯.

items.q: Where do you find your one small job for each day? The ____ list.
items.why: The task list tells you one job for each day.
items.no: It has a box to check for each job.
items.hint: It starts with t.

items.q: How many of your tries count for your score?
items.why: Only your first try counts. That is why we slow down and check.
no: You get three tries, but only the first one counts.
The last try does not count. The first one does.

notes.do: She types. Let her find the answers on her own by looking back if she needs to.
notes.ask: Why is it smart to check your answer before you press Check?
notes.listen: Because only the first try counts. If she says she will just try again, remind her: tries 2 and 3 help you learn, but they do not count.

slides.title: Number words
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: One number symbol: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9.
words.example: 547 has three digits: 5, 4 and 7.

words.meaning: What a digit is worth because of the place where it sits.
words.example: In 547, the 5 is in the hundreds place. Its place value is 500.

words.meaning: A number written the usual way.
words.example: 547 is in standard form.

words.meaning: A number split into what each digit is worth, with plus signs.
words.example: 500 + 40 + 7 is the expanded form of 547.

words.meaning: To change a number to the nearest ten or hundred. It makes the number easier to use.
words.example: 47 rounds up to 50.

notes.do: She reads each card aloud, flips it, then covers it and says the meaning in her own words.
notes.say: These five words are on your Pathways Week 1 Math lesson too. Learn them today and that lesson gets easier.
notes.ask: What is the difference between a digit and its value?
notes.listen: The digit is the symbol (5). The value is what it is worth (500). If she mixes them up, that is normal; the next slide fixes it.

slides.title: Every digit has a place
slides.text: Look at 547. Each digit sits in a place.

steps.text: The 5 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 500.
The 4 is in the tens place. It is worth 40.
The 7 is in the ones place. It is worth 7.

slides.tip: Read the places from the left: hundreds, tens, ones.

notes.do: Hands-on: she builds 547 on the place-value mat with 5 hundred squares, 4 ten strips and 7 ones. Then click the steps one at a time.
notes.say: The digit 5 is just a symbol. Where it sits tells us it is worth 500.
notes.ask: How many ones are in one ten strip? How many ones in one hundred square?
notes.listen: 10 and 100. If she counts, let her count one strip, then say: every strip is the same.

slides.title: Same digit, new value
slides.text: The digit 4 is in all three numbers. But it is worth something different each time.

steps.text: In 481, the 4 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 400.
In 148, the 4 is in the tens place. It is worth 40.
In 814, the 4 is in the ones place. It is worth just 4.

notes.do: She moves the same three digit cards (4, 8, 1) into new spots on the mat for each number.
notes.ask: Which 4 is worth the most? Which is worth the least?
notes.listen: The 4 in 481 (400) is worth the most; the 4 in 814 (4) the least. She should say the value, not just the digit.

slides.title: What is it worth?
slides.text: Say it out loud first. Then type.

items.q: In 362, what is the value of the 6?
items.why: The 6 is in the tens place. It is worth 60.
items.no: Find the 6. Which place is it in? Ones, tens or hundreds?
items.hint: 6 tens = 60.

items.q: In 815, which digit is in the hundreds place?
items.why: 815: 8 hundreds, 1 ten, 5 ones. The hundreds digit is 8.
items.no: Say the places from the left: hundreds, tens, ones.
items.hint: Type just one digit.

items.q: Which number has a 9 that is worth 900?
items.why: In 962, the 9 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 900.
no: In 498, the 9 is in the tens place. It is worth 90.
In 239, the 9 is in the ones place. It is worth 9.

notes.do: She says the place and the value out loud before she types: "The 6 is in the tens place, so it is worth 60."
notes.listen: 60, 8, and 962. If she types 6 for the first one, ask: which place is the 6 in? What is one ten strip worth?

slides.title: Standard form and expanded form
slides.text:
486 is in standard form. That is the usual way.
Expanded form splits it into what each digit is worth.

steps.text: 4 hundreds = 400. 8 tens = 80. 6 ones = 6.
Now look at 609. There are 0 tens.
We still write the 0: 609 = 600 + 0 + 9.
A 0 holds the place. Without it, 609 would turn into 69!

slides.tip: Expanded form always has three parts for a 3-digit number, even when one part is 0.

notes.do: She builds 609 on the mat: 6 hundred squares, nothing in the tens column, 9 ones. Point to the empty tens column.
notes.say: The tens column is empty, so we write 0 there. The 0 is a place holder.
notes.ask: What number do you get if you forget the 0 in 609?
notes.listen: 69. That is a much smaller number. This is the mistake Pathways tests with numbers like 900 + 0 + 6.

slides.title: Expand it
slides.text: Use your mat if you need it.

items.why: 273 = 200 + 70 + 3. The missing part is 70.
items.no: Write what each digit is worth, not just the digit.
items.hint: Which place is missing? What is that digit worth?

items.why: 5 hundreds, 0 tens, 2 ones = 502.
items.no: Put one digit in each place: hundreds, tens, ones.
items.hint: A 0 tens still needs a 0 in the tens place.

no: That makes 1,100, not 830. The 3 is in the tens place, so it is worth 30.
That only lists the digits. Write what each digit is worth.
That makes 803, not 830. Check what the middle digit is worth.

notes.do: For the second one she builds 500 + 0 + 2 on the mat before typing.
notes.listen: 70, 502, and 800 + 30 + 0. If she types 52 for the second one, she skipped the 0 tens: point to the empty tens column.

slides.title: Round to the nearest ten
slides.text: Rounding finds the closest ten. Look at the ones digit.

steps.text: 36 is between 30 and 40. The ones digit is 6. 6 is 5 or more, so round up to 40.
33 is between 30 and 40. The ones digit is 3. 3 is 4 or less, so stay down at 30.
35 is right in the middle. The rule says 5 goes up: 40.
Bigger numbers work the same way. 128 is between 120 and 130. The ones digit is 8, so round up to 130.

slides.tip: 5 or more, go up. 4 or less, stay down.

notes.do: Draw a hill on the whiteboard: 30 at the bottom left, 35 at the top, 40 at the bottom right. Numbers past the top roll down to 40; numbers before it roll back to 30.
notes.say: When we round, we only change to a ten. 36 cannot round to 35. It has to be 30 or 40.
notes.ask: Which two tens is 128 between? How do you know?
notes.listen: 120 and 130, because there are 12 tens. If she says 100 and 200, she is rounding to the hundred; remind her: nearest ten means the tens next door.

slides.title: Round to the nearest ten
slides.text: Find the two tens. Look at the ones digit. Then type.

items.why: 64 is between 60 and 70. The ones digit is 4. 4 or less, so stay down: 60.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more goes up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: It is between 60 and 70. Which one is it closer to?

items.why: 25 is between 20 and 30. The ones digit is 5. 5 or more, so round up: 30.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more goes up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: It is between 20 and 30. Which one is it closer to?

items.why: 237 is between 230 and 240. The ones digit is 7. 5 or more, so round up: 240.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more goes up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: It is between 230 and 240. Which one is it closer to?

notes.do: Before each answer she says the two tens out loud: "64 is between 60 and 70."
notes.listen: 60, 30, 240. If she types 65 or 25, she kept the number or rounded to a 5; remind her: rounding always lands on a ten.

slides.title: Round to the nearest hundred
slides.text: Same rule. But now look at the tens digit.

steps.text: 437 is between 400 and 500. The tens digit is 3. Stay down: 400.
462 is between 400 and 500. The tens digit is 6. Round up: 500.
650 is between 600 and 700. The tens digit is 5. 5 goes up: 700.

slides.tip: Nearest ten: look at the ones. Nearest hundred: look at the tens.

notes.do: Cover the ones digit with a finger for each number, so only the hundreds and tens show.
notes.say: For hundreds, the ones digit does not matter. Only the tens digit decides.
notes.ask: Why does 437 round to 400 and not 440?
notes.listen: 440 is the nearest ten. We asked for the nearest hundred, so it has to be 400 or 500.

slides.title: Round to the nearest hundred
slides.text: Cover the ones digit. Look at the tens digit.

items.why: 318 is between 300 and 400. The tens digit is 1. 4 or less, so stay down: 300.
items.no: For hundreds, look at the tens digit.
items.hint: It is between 300 and 400. Look at the tens digit.

items.why: 581 is between 500 and 600. The tens digit is 8. 5 or more, so round up: 600.
items.no: For hundreds, look at the tens digit.
items.hint: It is between 500 and 600. Look at the tens digit.

items.q: The DeSoto library has 352 picture books. About how many is that, rounded to the nearest hundred?
items.why: 352 is between 300 and 400. The tens digit is 5, so it rounds to 400.
no: 350 is 352 rounded to the nearest ten. This one asks for the nearest hundred.
The tens digit is 5. That is 5 or more, so round up.

notes.do: She says which two hundreds each number is between before she types.
notes.listen: 300, 600, 400. If she picks 350 for the books, she rounded to the nearest ten; ask: is 350 a hundred?

slides.title: Theo's First Hike
slides.text: This is the story from your Pathways Week 1 Reading lesson. Read it with me.

visual.text:
Theo's First Hike (part 1, short)
Theo laced up his brand-new hiking boots. He checked his backpack twice. He clipped his father's old compass to his belt loop. Theo had never been on a real trail before. His hands were a little shaky. But he could not stop smiling. Today was different. Today was real.

prompts: What does Theo do to get ready?
How does Theo feel? Which words tell you?

notes.do: Open the real Pathways Week 1 Reading story if you want her to see the full version. Read this short part together: you read a sentence, she reads the next. Give her 4 to 5 minutes to talk. Tap the gold button for each strong answer.
notes.say: This is the story you will see again when you retake Pathways Week 1 Reading. Today we read it like detectives.
notes.ask: His hands are shaky, but he is smiling. What does each clue tell you about how he feels?
notes.listen: Yes: nervous (shaky hands) and excited (smiling). She scored 56 on this lesson, so take it slow and praise every clue she finds.

slides.title: Story words
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word and the meaning out loud.

words.meaning: A person or animal in a story. The main character is who the story is mostly about.
words.example: Theo is the main character in Theo's First Hike.

words.meaning: Where and when a story happens.
words.example: The setting is a forest trail in the early morning.

words.meaning: A word that tells what a character is like inside.
words.example: Kind, brave and curious are traits.

words.meaning: The voice that tells the story.
words.example: The narrator tells us that Theo's hands were shaky.

words.meaning: To use clues to figure out something the story does not say.
words.example: The story never says "brave." I infer it from what Theo does.

notes.do: Same routine: read, flip, cover, say it in her own words.
notes.ask: Is a trait the same as a feeling? (Close: a feeling can change fast; a trait is what someone is like most of the time.)
notes.listen: Setting must include WHEN as well as WHERE. If she only says "the woods", ask: what time of day was it?

slides.title: Character clues
slides.text: Good readers look for 3 kinds of clues about a character.

steps.text: 👟 What the character does. Theo laces his boots. He checks his backpack twice.
💭 What the character says or thinks. Theo thinks: Today was different. Today was real.
❤️ What the character feels. Shaky hands = nervous. Big smile = excited.
Put the clues together: Theo is nervous and excited about his first hike.

slides.tip: Does, says, feels. Look for all three.

notes.do: Draw a 3-column chart on the whiteboard: DOES / SAYS-THINKS / FEELS. She fills it in from the Theo passage with you.
notes.ask: Why do you think he checked his backpack twice?
notes.listen: He wants to be ready, or he is a little nervous. Either is a good inference if she gives the clue.

slides.title: Setting: where and when
slides.text: The setting is where and when the story happens.

visual.text:
Theo's First Hike (part 2, short)
The trail went through tall pine trees. It dipped down past a rocky creek. Then it climbed up toward Lookout Peak. It was early morning. A soft mist hung low over the valley.

steps.text: 📍 Where: a trail with tall pine trees, a rocky creek and Lookout Peak.
⏰ When: early morning.
🌫️ Weather: misty. The mist makes the story feel quiet and a little mysterious.

slides.tip: Things a character carries, like a compass, are not the setting.

notes.do: She underlines (points to) every WHERE word in one color and every WHEN word in another as you read the passage aloud together.
notes.ask: Is Theo's compass part of the setting?
notes.listen: No. It is something Theo has. The setting is the place and the time. This is a Boss Battle question type in Pathways.

slides.title: Character or setting?
slides.text: A new story: Nia's Big Game. Tap a card. Then tap the right box.
buckets:
🧒 Character clue
who and what they are like

items.text: Nia ties her soccer cleats tight.
items.why: That is something Nia does.
items.hint: Is it a person doing something, or a place or time?

items.why: That is where the story happens.
items.hint: Is it a place?

items.why: That tells when.
items.hint: Does it tell a time?

items.why: That is something Nia does.
items.hint: Who is doing it?

items.text: Nia feels nervous before the game.
items.why: That is how Nia feels.
items.hint: Is it a feeling?

items.why: That is part of the place.
items.hint: Can you stand in it or see it around you?

slides.done: Character = who. Setting = where and when.

notes.do: She reads each card out loud before she sorts it.
notes.ask: Which card was the hardest? Why?
notes.listen: Often "bleachers full of parents": the parents are people, but here they are part of the place around Nia, not the main character.

slides.title: Infer a trait
slides.text: A story does not always say what a character is like. We infer it from clues.

visual.text:
Theo's First Hike (part 3, short)
Halfway up, Theo's legs began to ache. He wondered if he should turn back. Then he remembered his grandfather. He took a breath and kept climbing.

steps.text: Clue 1: His legs ache. The hike is hard.
Clue 2: He thinks about turning back.
Clue 3: He keeps climbing anyway.
The story never says "brave" or "determined." But the clues show it. Theo is determined: he keeps going when it is hard.

slides.tip: One clue is a guess. Many clues make a strong inference.

notes.do: She holds up one finger for each clue as you reveal it.
notes.say: Determined means you keep going even when something is hard.
notes.ask: Do you know someone who is determined? What do they do?
notes.listen: A real example with an action ("my mom keeps trying"). Connect it: you can be determined on your Pathways retake too.

slides.title: Be a story detective
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text:
At the Park
Marcus was at the park after school. A little boy dropped his ice cream. The boy started to cry. Marcus walked over. He gave the boy half of his own cone.

items.why: Marcus shares his own cone with a crying boy. That shows he is kind.
no: Lazy means not wanting to do things. Marcus walks over to help.
Bossy means telling others what to do. Marcus does not do that.

choices: He gave the boy half of his own cone.
The little boy dropped his ice cream and started to cry.
items.why: Giving away half of his own cone is what Marcus does. It shows he is kind.
no: That is the setting. It does not tell what Marcus is like.
That is what the little boy did, not Marcus.

items.q: Is the park after school a clue about the character or the setting? Type character or setting.
items.why: The park after school tells where and when. It is the setting.
items.no: Character = who. Setting = where and when.
items.hint: Is it a person or animal? Or is it a place or a time?

notes.do: She reads the story aloud first. Then she answers on her own.
notes.listen: kind; the cone clue; setting. If she picks "Marcus was at the park" as the clue, ask: does being at the park tell us he is kind?

slides.title: Check for understanding
slides.text: On your own now. No help.

items.q: In 726, what is the value of the 2?
items.why: The 2 is in the tens place. It is worth 20.
items.no: Find the 2. Which place is it in? Ones, tens or hundreds?
items.hint: 2 tens = 20.

items.why: 465 is between 400 and 500. The tens digit is 6. 5 or more, so round up: 500.
items.no: For hundreds, look at the tens digit.
items.hint: It is between 400 and 500. Look at the tens digit.

items.q: A story happens at a zoo on a hot afternoon. The zoo and the afternoon are the story's ____.
items.why: The zoo is where. The hot afternoon is when. Where and when = the setting.
items.no: Which story word means where and when?
items.hint: It starts with s.

items.q:
Read: Lena's hands shook as she held the puppy for the first time. Then she smiled. She hugged the puppy close.
How does Lena feel?
items.why: Shaking hands are a clue for nervous. Smiling and hugging are clues for happy.
no: Nothing in the story shows angry or sad. Look at her hands and her smile.
She is not bored. Her hands shake, then she smiles.

notes.do: Hands off. Note her first answers on paper.
notes.listen: 20, 500, setting, nervous then happy. All four right means she is ready for the after-class lesson tonight. Two or more wrong: go back to that slide for 3 minutes before wrap-up.

Wednesday: Practice. Thursday: Packet page 1.
Friday: retake Pathways Week 1 Reading, Theo's First Hike. Look back at the story before you answer.
Saturday: Packet page 2. Sunday: Practice again.

notes.do: Open her course page and read the task list together, one day at a time. Have her check off nothing yet; show her where the boxes are. Point out the two OPTIONAL Science and Social Studies links and say they are only if she wants more.
notes.say: You did great today. Look at the goal you told me at the start. This week is your first block toward it.
notes.ask: What do you do tonight? What do you do on Friday?
notes.listen: Tonight: the after-class lesson. Friday: the Pathways reading retake. Tell her to aim for 85 and to type 1111 if a Pathways lesson is locked.

slides.title: Place value and rounding

steps.text: Nearest ten: look at the ones digit. 538 → 540.
Nearest hundred: look at the tens digit. 538 → 500.

slides.tip: 5 or more, go up. 4 or less, stay down.

slides.title: Place value
slides.text: Say the place. Then type the answer.

items.q: In 172, what is the value of the 7?
items.why: The 7 is in the tens place. It is worth 70.
items.no: Find the 7. Which place is it in? Ones, tens or hundreds?
items.hint: 7 tens = 70.

items.q: In 905, which digit is in the tens place?
items.why: 905: 9 hundreds, 0 tens, 5 ones. The tens digit is 0.
items.no: Say the places from the left: hundreds, tens, ones.
items.hint: Type just one digit.

items.q: Which number has a 3 that is worth 30?
items.why: In 831, the 3 is in the tens place. It is worth 30.
no: In 357, the 3 is in the hundreds place. It is worth 300.
In 503, the 3 is in the ones place. It is worth 3.

slides.title: Expanded form
slides.text: Write what each digit is worth.

items.why: 694 = 600 + 90 + 4. The missing part is 4.
items.no: Write what each digit is worth, not just the digit.
items.hint: Which place is missing? What is that digit worth?

items.why: 7 hundreds, 0 tens, 1 one = 701.
items.no: Put one digit in each place: hundreds, tens, ones.
items.hint: A 0 tens still needs a 0 in the tens place.

no: That only lists the digits. Write what each digit is worth.
That makes 406, not 460. Check what the middle digit is worth.
That makes 1,000, not 460. The 6 is in the tens place, so it is worth 60.

slides.title: Round it
slides.text: Ten: look at the ones. Hundred: look at the tens.

items.why: 53 is between 50 and 60. The ones digit is 3. 4 or less, so stay down: 50.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more goes up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: It is between 50 and 60. Which one is it closer to?

items.why: 146 is between 140 and 150. The ones digit is 6. 5 or more, so round up: 150.
items.no: Look at the ones digit. 5 or more goes up. 4 or less stays.
items.hint: It is between 140 and 150. Which one is it closer to?

items.why: 729 is between 700 and 800. The tens digit is 2. 4 or less, so stay down: 700.
items.no: For hundreds, look at the tens digit.
items.hint: It is between 700 and 800. Look at the tens digit.

items.q: A park trail is 285 feet long. About how long is it, rounded to the nearest hundred?
items.why: 285 is between 200 and 300. The tens digit is 8, so it rounds to 300.
no: The tens digit is 8. That is 5 or more, so round up.
290 is 285 rounded to the nearest ten. This one asks for the nearest hundred.

slides.title: Story words
slides.text:
Character = who the story is about.
Setting = where and when it happens.

steps.text: A trait tells what a character is like: kind, brave, careful.
To infer, use clues: what the character does, says and feels.

slides.tip: Look back at the story. The clues are always in the words.

slides.title: Owen's Snow Day
slides.text: Read the story. Then answer.

visual.text:
Owen's Snow Day
Snow covered the farm. It was early morning, and the barn roof was white. Owen pulled on his red boots. He grabbed a shovel and cleared a path to the goat pen. He did not stop until the path was done.

items.q: Who is the main character? Type his name.
items.why: The story is about Owen.
items.no: Who does the most in the story?

choices: a farm on a snowy morning
the shovel Owen used to clear a path
items.why: Setting = where and when: a farm on a snowy morning.
no: Boots are something Owen wears. They are not where or when.
A shovel is something Owen uses. It is not where or when.

items.why: He shovels a whole path and does not stop until it is done. He is hardworking.

teacher.objective: Ce'Line learns how her Building Blocks course works (course page, class lesson, after-class lesson with Show What You Know, practice, packet, task list). Then she learns Pathways Week 1: she names the place and value of each digit in a 3-digit number, writes numbers in standard and expanded form (including a 0 place holder), rounds to the nearest ten (look at the ones digit) and nearest hundred (look at the tens digit), and finds the character, the setting (where AND when) and a character trait she infers from clues in Theo's First Hike and in new short stories.
materials: The class lesson on a laptop (teacher code 9110) and her course page open in a second tab
Paper place-value mat (Hundreds | Tens | Ones) and base-ten pieces or paper cut-outs: 9 hundred squares, 9 ten strips, 9 ones
Her Packet (2 pages), printed: page 1 Thursday, page 2 Saturday

plan.do: Class slide 1. Welcome her to her own course. Ask what she wants to get better at; write it in the corner of the whiteboard.
Class slides 2–3. Show her real course page in a second tab: the Lesson 1 card, each button, the task list and the Also do links. She types the quick check (85, task list, first try).
Class slide 4. Read, flip, cover, say it in her own words: digit, place value, standard form, expanded form, round.
Class slides 5–7. She builds 547 on the place-value mat, moves the 4 card to show 481 / 148 / 814, then answers 362, 815 and the 900 question.
Class slides 8–9. 486 = 400 + 80 + 6; 609 with the empty tens column. Then 273, 500 + 0 + 2 and 830.
Class slides 10–11. Rounding hill on the whiteboard. She names the two tens before every answer (64, 25, 237).
Class slides 12–13. Cover the ones digit. 318, 581 and the library's 352 books.
Class slide 14. Read the short part together, sentence by sentence. She talks about who, what he does and how he feels.
Class slide 15. character, setting, trait, narrator, infer.
Class slides 16–17. Does / says-thinks / feels chart on the whiteboard; where and when in Theo's trail.
Class slide 18. She reads each card aloud, then sorts it.
Class slides 19–20. Theo's clue chain (determined), then Marcus at the park on her own.
Class slide 21. On her own. Note her first answers.
Class slide 22. Read her task list together on the course page. Point out the OPTIONAL Science and Social Studies links. Remind her: aim for 85, type 1111 if a Pathways lesson is locked.

watch: Digit vs. value: asked for the value of the 6 in 362, she may type 6. Ask: which place is it in? What is one ten strip worth? Have her say the full sentence: "The 6 is in the tens place, so it is worth 60."

The 0 place holder: 500 + 0 + 2 written as 52, or 407 expanded as 400 + 7. Point to the empty column on the mat: the 0 holds the place. Pathways tests this in its Boss Battle (numbers like 306 and 504).
Rounding to a 5: typing 65 or 85 for "round 64 to the nearest ten." Rounding always lands on a ten (or a hundred). Have her name the two tens first.
Looking at the wrong digit: for the nearest hundred she must look at the tens digit, not the ones. If 437 becomes 440, she rounded to the nearest ten. Cover the ones digit with a finger.
The 5 rule: 35, 25, 450 and 650 all go up. If she rounds them down, repeat: 5 or more, go up.
Setting = where AND when: she may name only the place ("the woods"). Ask: what time of day? Also, things a character carries (Theo's compass, Jamal's flashlight) are not the setting.
Infer from the text, not from a guess: every trait answer needs a clue she can point to. Ask: which words told you that?

Confidence: her scores so far are low and she needs a lot of support. Praise every correct step out loud, keep your voice calm on wrong answers, and let her look back at the slide or the story before she answers.
